strengths: The core idea—learning endpoint-conditioned interpolants by adversarially matching observed intermediate marginals—is conceptually interesting and meaningfully different from pointwise multi-marginal interpolation.
The paper is generally well organized and connects the learned interpolants cleanly to conditional flow matching.
The evaluation covers synthetic, cell-tracking, scRNA-seq, and spatial-transcriptomics settings, including up to 100-dimensional data and many observation times.

The spatial-transcriptomics results are promising: OT-ALI-CFM obtains the best reported mean EMD (98.91 versus approximately 109 for the strongest alternatives) with substantially lower reported variability.
Useful implementation details, architectures, preprocessing descriptions, and baseline-training information are included in the appendix.
weaknesses: Theorem 2.2 and its proof appear invalid. The reference interpolation depends on the intermediate sample x_ti, whereas the optimized G is restricted to depend only on (x0,x1). The proposed optimizer G=T∘ell therefore generally depends on x_ti and is not an admissible endpoint-conditioned interpolant. The proof also assumes that arbitrary optimal couplings between the reference and target distributions are realizable under this information restriction. This undermines a prominent uniqueness claim.

The theoretical guarantees do not describe the actual finite-weight adversarial objective. They assume exact marginal constraints, while GAN training only approximates those constraints; uniqueness is pointwise in time and does not imply a unique or smooth trajectory across time. Theorem 2.1 also omits conditions such as finite second moments, and its proof contains an inconsistent expression G=T∘ell−ell.

The empirical evidence is insufficient for several central claims. The knot and cell-tracking experiments are evaluated almost entirely visually, with the authors explicitly omitting quantitative cell-tracking evaluation. There are no measurements of marginal matching, trajectory smoothness, CFM variance, divergence frequency, or computational cost.

Performance is mixed rather than clearly competitive. OT-ALI-CFM is not best on any scRNA-seq setting in Tables 1–2 and is substantially worse than OT-MFM in several high-dimensional cases. The spatial-transcriptomics claim relies on only four sections and two possible held-out marginals, without statistical significance testing or comparison to simple spatial interpolation, OT barycenters, or domain-specific reconstruction baselines.

Essential ablations are missing: adversarial matching versus non-adversarial distribution losses, each proposed regularizer, endpoint coupling choices, pretraining and time-noise heuristics, lambda sensitivity, GAN stability, and network/training-budget matching. The experiments also change the GAN formulation and regularizer across datasets, making it unclear which components drive performance.

The spatial-transcriptomics protocol uses manual nonlinear registration involving every section, including the held-out one, and selects the tumor threshold through visual agreement. The intended test-time information and possible leakage from the held-out image should be specified and controlled.

Reproducibility remains limited: no code or trained-model release is identified, seeds and hardware are unspecified, some reported uncertainties are not clearly defined, and Algorithm 1 does not correctly spell out the opposing generator/discriminator optimization directions.

strengths: The central idea—learning endpoint-conditioned interpolants by adversarially matching their intermediate pushforward distributions—is conceptually interesting and meaningfully different from pointwise multi-marginal interpolation.
The method is presented clearly, with an explicit interpolant parameterization, two-stage training procedure, pseudocode, and several regularization choices.

The experiments cover synthetic data, cell tracking, single-cell RNA sequencing, and spatial transcriptomics, demonstrating broad potential applicability. Many architectural and optimization details are supplied.
ALI-CFM produces promising qualitative results on the knot and cell-tracking examples and obtains the best reported average EMD on the spatial-transcriptomics experiment.
weaknesses: The claimed uniqueness theory is overstated and appears technically flawed. In Theorem 2.2, the proposed optimal solution T composed with the piecewise-linear reference generally depends on the intermediate sample x_ti, whereas the admissible interpolant G is restricted to depend only on (x0,x1,t). The proof does not establish that the optimal transport map factors through the endpoint pair, so existence and uniqueness within the stated function class do not follow. More broadly, both theorems concern exact constrained population optimization, not the penalized GAN objective or its neural-network solutions, and therefore do not justify the repeated claim that the practical regularizers guarantee unique interpolants.

The empirical evidence is insufficient for the paper's strongest claims. The knot and cell-tracking experiments are assessed almost entirely through selected visualizations; the assertion that these are conclusive is not a substitute for quantitative marginal accuracy, trajectory error, smoothness, divergence, or robustness measurements. The cell-tracking evaluation additionally uses only one tracked cell sequence.

The scRNA-seq results are unfavorable overall: ALI-CFM loses to OT-MFM on every 5D dataset and to both OT-MFM and OT-CFM in all reported 50D/100D settings. Consequently, the claimed scalability and state-of-the-art competitiveness are not convincingly demonstrated, especially without runtime or memory measurements.

The spatial-transcriptomics evidence is narrow, comprising one specimen, four sections, and only two possible held-out intermediate sections. The improvement over OT-CFM/OT-MMFM is modest relative to the reported variability, with no statistical test or per-split results. Manual nonlinear alignment, use of the target section's image during alignment, and a purity threshold chosen by visual agreement also weaken reproducibility and complicate the interpretation as inference of an unobserved section.

Essential ablations are missing: adversarial matching versus simpler distributional objectives such as MMD or Sinkhorn losses; contributions of the coupling, each regularizer, pretraining, time noise, LAND metric, and GAN variant; sensitivity to lambda and other tuned hyperparameters; and measurements of GAN instability or mode collapse. The final experiments also depart from the vanilla GAN objective analyzed in the method by using R3GAN, without isolating its effect.

The comparison protocol is incompletely controlled. Network sizes and training budgets differ substantially, a multi-marginal MFM variant is excluded from the spatial experiment based only on unreported preliminary tests, and the paper does not report parameter counts, compute, or systematic baseline tuning.

Matching snapshot marginals does not identify the underlying trajectories. The paper does not adequately discuss this fundamental ambiguity, yet repeatedly frames the output as recovering dynamics or trajectories; most evaluations measure only held-out marginal EMD and therefore cannot validate those stronger claims.

Reproducibility remains limited despite the hyperparameter appendix: no code or trained models are supplied, some implementation choices are described only informally, and the manually aligned spatial-transcriptomics preprocessing cannot be reconstructed from the manuscript alone.

strengths: The paper introduces a clear and meaningful idea: learning endpoint-conditioned interpolants by adversarially matching their intermediate marginals to observed snapshot distributions, followed by conditional flow matching. This distribution-level formulation is a useful alternative to methods that force trajectories through individual samples.
The method is broadly applicable to discrete or densely sampled time points and is demonstrated on synthetic data, cell tracking, single-cell RNA sequencing, and spatial transcriptomics.

The knot and cell-tracking examples compellingly illustrate a regime in which smooth, time-dependent interpolants can be preferable to piecewise-linear, spline-based, or time-independent-metric alternatives.
The spatial-transcriptomics experiment is promising: OT-ALI-CFM obtains the best reported EMD, with lower variance than the compared methods.

The presentation is generally clear, with helpful algorithms, visualizations, and substantial implementation detail in the appendix. The paper also candidly reports that the method does not outperform the strongest baseline on the single-cell benchmarks.
weaknesses: Theorem 2.2 appears technically incorrect as proved. Its proposed optimizer G=T∘ℓ depends on the intermediate sample x_ti through ℓ, whereas the admissible G is defined to depend only on (x0,x1,t). Unless x_ti is deterministic given the endpoints, the optimal transport map constructed in the proof need not belong to the feasible function class. The appropriate reduction would involve the conditional mean of ℓ given (x0,x1), not ℓ itself.

The uniqueness results concern exact constrained marginal matching followed by regularizer minimization. The implemented objective is instead a finite-weight, nonconvex GAN penalty, so these results do not establish uniqueness of the learned neural interpolants. The abstract and discussion overstate this guarantee. Even pointwise uniqueness at observed times would not establish uniqueness or smoothness of the complete trajectory between those times.

The empirical evidence is uneven. The synthetic and cell-tracking experiments rely almost entirely on selected visualizations, with the paper explicitly declining quantitative evaluation because the plots are considered conclusive. There are no trajectory errors, marginal discrepancies, smoothness measures, divergence rates, or repeated-run statistics for these key experiments.

On the established single-cell benchmarks, OT-MFM outperforms OT-ALI-CFM in every reported 5D task and every reported 50D/100D task. OT-ALI-CFM is also worse than the simpler OT-CFM in most high-dimensional settings. Thus, running the method at high dimension demonstrates feasibility but does not provide strong evidence for competitive scalability or accuracy.

The paper lacks essential ablations: adversarial matching versus non-adversarial distribution losses, each proposed regularizer, regularization weight, endpoint coupling, time-input noise, pretraining, R3GAN versus the stated vanilla GAN objective, and sensitivity or failure rates of adversarial optimization. These components differ substantially across datasets, making it unclear which parts of ALI-CFM drive the gains.

The spatial-transcriptomics result is based on one specimen with only four manually registered sections and two possible held-out slices. The uncertainty calculation is not explained, statistical significance is not assessed, and the manual nonlinear alignment and visually selected tumor-purity threshold limit reproducibility and risk introducing evaluation-specific choices.

Baseline comparisons are difficult to audit because architectures, training budgets, coupling choices, and tuning procedures vary across methods and tasks. Computational cost is not reported despite ALI-CFM requiring a separate generator, discriminator, pretraining stage, and flow network.

Several strong claims—including outperforming existing baselines on cell tracking, robustness to noise, stable GAN training, and superior handling of large numbers of marginals—are not supported by quantitative comparisons or robustness studies. Code, seeds, complete alignment landmarks, and sufficient information to reproduce the manual preprocessing are also not provided.

strengths: The paper proposes an interesting and conceptually distinct approach to multi-marginal flow matching: learning endpoint-conditioned interpolants by adversarially matching their intermediate marginal distributions rather than forcing paths through individual intermediate samples.
ALI-CFM is clearly motivated, and the two-stage construction—learning interpolants and then marginalizing them through conditional flow matching—is generally understandable.
The empirical study spans synthetic data, cell tracking, single-cell transcriptomics, and spatial transcriptomics, demonstrating broad applicability and the ability to handle many observation times.
The spatial transcriptomics experiment shows a promising EMD improvement, and the appendix provides substantial architecture, optimization, and hyperparameter information.
weaknesses: Theorem 2.2 and its proof appear incorrect. The reference path depends on the intermediate sample x_ti, whereas G is restricted to depend only on (x0,x1). The proof nevertheless concludes G=T∘ell, whose right-hand side generally depends on x_ti and therefore need not define a function of the endpoints. Absolute continuity of ell#pi_ti is insufficient for the claimed existence and uniqueness under this restricted function class.

Equation (12) does not define a valid piecewise-linear interpolation after t_i: its second branch lacks the required (t-t_i) coefficient, so it generally neither equals x_ti at t_i nor x1 at t=1. Theorem 2.1's proof also writes G=T∘ell−ell when the optimal interpolant should be T∘ell. These errors undermine the main theoretical presentation.

The stated uniqueness guarantees concern exact distribution constraints and ideal optimization over unrestricted functions. They do not establish uniqueness for the finite-weight penalized GAN objective, its neural parameterization, or its nonconvex training procedure. Moreover, matching finitely many observed marginals does not uniquely determine the curve between observation times.

The quantitative results are not consistently competitive. OT-ALI-CFM loses to OT-MFM on every 5D single-cell dataset and is substantially worse than OT-CFM and OT-MFM in most 50D/100D settings. Thus the scalability experiment demonstrates executability more clearly than competitive accuracy.

The knot and cell-tracking claims rely largely on visual examples. The cell-tracking study uses one cell trajectory and explicitly omits quantitative evaluation, while claims about smoothness, gradient variance, and divergence lack systematic metrics, uncertainty estimates, or robustness tests.

The spatial transcriptomics result averages a very small leave-one-section-out experiment, with unclear decomposition of the reported uncertainty and no significance analysis. Manual nonlinear registration and visually selected tumor thresholds also introduce subjective preprocessing and possible sensitivity that is not evaluated.

The experimental protocol leaves fairness and reproducibility concerns: the proposed method receives task-specific objectives, regularizers, pretraining, noise injection, and extensive tuning; baseline architectures and training budgets differ; and no implementation release for ALI-CFM is identified. Algorithm 1 also obscures the alternating min-max optimization by describing a joint gradient update.

strengths: The paper proposes a relevant and conceptually appealing idea: learn a single smooth neural interpolant by adversarially matching observed intermediate marginal distributions, then marginalize it using conditional flow matching.
The method targets an important snapshot-data setting and is evaluated on varied domains, including synthetic dynamics, cell tracking, single-cell data, and spatial transcriptomics.
The endpoint-preserving parameterization is simple, and the separation between interpolant learning and vector-field learning is clearly presented.
The appendices provide substantial implementation detail, dataset information, and regularizer ablations.
weaknesses: The theoretical uniqueness claims are not established as written. In Theorem 2.1's proof, the claimed solution G=T∘ℓ−ℓ generally does not push forward to q_t; it should instead be T∘ℓ. More seriously, the construction for Theorem 2.2 depends on the intermediate sample x_{t_i}, although the optimized interpolant G is restricted to depend only on (x_0,x_1,t). With non-degenerate conditional intermediate samples, the proposed construction is not a feasible G of the stated form.

Equation (12), which defines the piecewise-linear reference used in a principal experiment, appears incorrect: its second branch uses [t x_1+(1−t)x_{t_i}]/(1−t_i). This does not equal x_{t_i} at t=t_i or x_1 at t=1. It should contain coefficients involving t−t_i. This makes the stated method and theory internally inconsistent unless it is merely a consequential typesetting error.

The uniqueness results concern an exact marginal constraint followed by regularizer minimization. The implemented finite-weight GAN objective neither enforces that constraint exactly nor inherits the claimed uniqueness. Thus the repeated claim that the regularizers guarantee unique learned interpolants is substantially stronger than the theory supports.

The quantitative evidence does not support broad superiority. OT-MFM is better on every 5D single-cell dataset in Table 1 and every high-dimensional setting in Table 2; OT-ALI-CFM is also worse than OT-CFM in three of four high-dimensional comparisons. The positive cell-tracking result uses one cell sequence and only visual assessment, while the synthetic study is likewise predominantly qualitative.

The spatial-transcriptomics evidence is narrow: it uses four manually aligned sections from one specimen, yielding only two leave-one-section-out prediction tasks. The reported improvement is therefore insufficient to substantiate general claims about tumor-coordinate inference, especially given manual nonlinear registration and a visually selected tumor-purity threshold.

Baseline fairness is difficult to assess because architectures, training budgets, coupling implementations, and hyperparameter searches differ substantially. A multi-marginal MFM variant is omitted based only on unspecified preliminary tests, and there are no matched-compute comparisons or sensitivity analyses for adversarial training.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite extensive hyperparameter descriptions. The experiments depart from the main vanilla-GAN formulation through R3GAN, pretraining, time noise, LAND-based regularization, and heuristically rescaled losses, but several of these choices are not fully specified and no code or complete stability analysis is provided.

Matching finitely many snapshot marginals cannot identify the underlying trajectories without strong structural assumptions. The regularizers select one admissible interpolation, but the paper sometimes describes this as recovering the underlying dynamics without demonstrating trajectory-level ground truth or acknowledging the associated identifiability limitation.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and potentially useful idea: learning a single global interpolant by adversarially matching observed intermediate marginals, followed by conditional flow matching. This distribution-level approach is meaningfully different from forcing trajectories through individual observations.

The method is tested on a diverse collection of synthetic, cell-tracking, single-cell, and spatial-transcriptomics problems. The knot and cell-tracking examples provide intuitive evidence that the learned interpolants can remain smooth when piecewise alternatives become unstable.
The spatial-transcriptomics experiment is an interesting application, and ALI-CFM obtains the best reported EMD, 98.91 versus approximately 109 for the strongest non-MFM baselines.
The presentation is generally clear, with helpful algorithms, visualizations, implementation details, and ablations over several regularizers.
weaknesses: The claimed uniqueness guarantee does not apply to the actual regularized GAN objective: Theorems 2.1–2.2 assume exact marginal matching as a hard constraint, whereas Eq. 8 trades adversarial divergence against regularization with a finite weight. Consequently, its optimizer need not satisfy the constraint and need not be unique.

The proof of Theorem 2.2 has a substantive measurability gap. The proposed optimizer T(l(x0,xti,x1,t)) generally depends on the intermediate sample xti, while the theorem requires G to be a function only of (x0,x1,t). A general Markov-chained coupling does not make xti recoverable from the endpoints. Additional deterministic/invertibility assumptions or a reformulated interpolant are required. Theorem 2.1's proof also contains an apparent erroneous expression G=T∘l−l.

The empirical evidence is uneven. The cell-tracking conclusions are based only on visual inspection despite known ground-truth segmentations at every frame. The knot experiment also lacks quantitative errors and variability, limiting support for the claimed superiority and stability.

ALI-CFM is consistently worse than OT-MFM in the main single-cell evaluation, often by a substantial margin in 50D and 100D. Thus the stated scalability and state-of-the-art competitiveness claims are not convincingly supported by the quantitative results.

The spatial-transcriptomics result is based on one specimen with only four manually and nonlinearly aligned sections. The meaning of the reported standard deviations, number of repetitions, and statistical significance are unclear, and the evaluation may be sensitive to the manually chosen alignment and tumour-purity threshold.

Reproducibility and fairness remain incomplete: no code artifact is identified, some tuning rules are vague (for example, scaling a regularizer to the generator-loss range), computational cost and GAN stability are not systematically reported, and baseline failures are sometimes inferred from selected visual runs. These issues, combined with the flawed theoretical claim, place the work below the acceptance bar despite the promising core idea.
